name: Alamandine
lead: Alamandine is a heptapeptide of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS), the hormone network that regulates blood pressure, fluid and electrolyte balance. It was characterised in 2013 and is formed from angiotensin A by ACE2, or directly from angiotensin-(1-7).[1][5]

It acts mainly through the MrgD receptor and, in laboratory studies, produces effects that oppose those of angiotensin II, such as vasorelaxation and protection against cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis in animals.[1][5] Published work is preclinical; no human clinical trial of alamandine as a treatment was found, and no source reviewed documents appearance-related use.[5]

paras: The 2013 Circulation Research paper reported identification of alamandine by mass spectrometry, showed that it circulates in human blood, and described its generation by ACE2 from angiotensin A or from angiotensin-(1-7).[1] Wikipedia notes that an earlier 2007 report had detected the peptide in human plasma.[5]

Reviews place alamandine in the protective arm of the RAS alongside ACE2, angiotensin-(1-7) and the Mas receptor, whose actions generally counteract angiotensin II in the heart, kidney and vasculature.[2][4][7] Related work examines the MAS-related receptor family to which MrgD belongs.[3]

According to the encyclopedia summary of the literature, alamandine produced endothelium-dependent vessel relaxation, lowered blood pressure in hypertensive rats, and reduced cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis in mice under pressure overload; mice lacking MrgD developed dilated cardiomyopathy. These results come from cells and rodents.[5]

No studies found. Published research on alamandine consists of laboratory and animal studies; the encyclopedia entry reports higher circulating levels in people with end-stage renal disease, which is an observation rather than a treatment trial.[5]

timeline.event: Peptide first detected in human plasma by mass spectrometry (per Wikipedia).[5]
Alamandine characterised as a new RAS component.[1]

card.summary: A blood-pressure-regulating peptide of the renin-angiotensin system; interesting cardiovascular biology in rodents, no human trials.
card.note: Preclinical only; no human therapeutic data.

quick.overview:
Alamandine is a small peptide made in the body as part of the renin-angiotensin system. It was described in 2013 and appears to counterbalance the blood-pressure-raising arm of that system.

Evidence for any effect comes from cell and rodent experiments. It is listed among longevity-category peptides, but no human trials have tested it.
quick.mechanism: It is generated by ACE2 from angiotensin A (or from angiotensin-(1-7)) and signals mainly through the MrgD receptor, producing vasorelaxation and anti-fibrotic effects in animals.[1][5]
quick.risks: No human safety data exist. Because it influences blood pressure and vascular tone in animals, effects in people are unstudied. It is not an approved drug.
